title: Fewest Cameras to Watch a Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. You may place cameras on nodes. A camera on a node watches that node, its parent and its direct children.

Return the smallest number of cameras that together watch every node. The node values do not matter.

Trees are written in level order with null for missing children: [0, 0, null, 0] is a root with a left child, which has a left child of its own.

examples.why: One camera on the root's child watches the root above it and both leaves below it.
A chain of 5 nodes. Cameras on the 2nd and 4th nodes cover everything. Putting one on every leaf's parent is the idea; one camera can never watch more than 3 nodes of a chain.
A single node still needs a camera on itself.

hints: Look at a leaf. Is it ever better to put the camera on the leaf rather than on its parent?

A camera on a leaf's parent watches the leaf, the parent, the parent's other child and the grandparent: a superset of what the leaf camera watches. So work bottom-up and place cameras as late (as high) as possible.

Post-order, each node reports one of three states: 'not watched yet', 'has a camera', or 'watched, no camera'. A null child counts as watched. If any child is not watched, put a camera here. Else if any child has a camera, this node is watched. Else report 'not watched' and let the parent deal with it. At the end, add a camera if the root is not watched.

explain.intuition:
Start from the leaves. A leaf must be watched, either by a camera on itself or on its parent. The parent is always at least as good: it watches the leaf too, plus the parent itself, its other child and the grandparent. So never put cameras on leaves; put them one level up. Then remove everything that is now watched and repeat the same argument higher up.

A post-order DFS does this in one pass. Each node returns a state to its parent: needs watching, has a camera or watched without a camera. A node whose child needs watching must take a camera, because nobody else can reach that child anymore. A node with a camera child is watched for free. A node whose children are both just watched leaves itself to its parent, which covers it with a camera placed as high as possible. Empty children report 'watched', so leaves correctly ask their parent for help. The root has no parent, so if it still needs watching it gets its own camera.
steps: Define visit(node) returning 0 = needs watching, 1 = has a camera, 2 = watched without a camera. A null node returns 2.
Compute the states of both children first (post-order).
If either child is 0, place a camera here: count it and return 1.
Else if either child is 1, return 2.
Else return 0. After visit(root), add one camera if the root returned 0.
pitfalls: Treating a null child as 'needs watching'. Then every leaf would get a camera.
Forgetting the root. If it returns 'needs watching', there is no parent to cover it.
Checking 'has a camera child' before 'needs watching child'. A node with one camera child and one unwatched child still needs its own camera.

solutions.title: Try every set of cameras
solutions.idea: For small trees, try every subset of nodes from the smallest, and return the size of the first one that watches every node.

solutions.title: Tree DP with three states
solutions.idea: For each node compute the cheapest cost when it has a camera, when a child's camera watches it, and when it is left for its parent to watch.

solutions.title: Greedy post-order
solutions.idea: Bottom-up, put a camera only on a node that has an unwatched child. Leaves ask their parent; the root may need its own camera.

followups: Each node now has a price for placing a camera there. Which of the two fast solutions still works?
Solve the same problem for a general tree given as an edge list.
